title: The Misting Machine
sendTrigger: Send this to whoever does the groceries.
editorialNotes: Do not add a percentage anywhere: the "up to 25% more expensive" misting figure traces to blogs, not a study (per the brief). The weight claim is mechanism only.
Thread progress is story progress (monotonic); the on-screen readout resetting on slide 7-8 is a visual state, not a progress reversal.

thread.element: produce scale readout creeping upward then resetting
thread.endState: readout resets to 1.00 LB with a dry weight tag

copy.headline: The mist is not for the vegetables. It is for you.
Produce is sold by the pound.
The misters run on timers, not on need.
items: Some chains pair them with a recorded thunder cue.
Wet produce looks plumper, glossier, and fresher than dry produce, and shoppers reach for it.

copy.headline: That water evaporates in your fridge within a day.
copy.body: You paid for it at the register. It does not come back off the receipt.

copy.headline: Here is the part that costs you twice.
items: Misting is not good for all types of produce.
On the wrong items the added moisture speeds up spoilage instead of slowing it.
copy.citation: Penn State Agricultural Sciences, on misting and produce type.

copy.headline: Misting helps: leafy greens, herbs, broccoli, celery, anything with an exposed cut surface.
copy.body: Misting hurts: berries, mushrooms, peppers, citrus, squash, anything with a skin that holds water against itself.

copy.headline: Three moves, none of them cost anything.
items: Shake it off over the case before you weigh it.
Dry the skinned items before they go in the fridge.
Line the crisper drawer with a paper towel and change it when it is damp.

copy.headline: You are not buying fresher vegetables. You are buying wetter ones.
copy.ctaLine: Know what you brought home, and how long it actually has.
